title: See Amid the Winter's Snow
description: Edward Caswall's Christmas hymn to John Goss's tune Humility, as Bramley and Stainer's Christmas Carols New and Old prints it, for 2 to 4 singers: verses 1, 2, 5 and 6, each with the chorus "Hail! Thou ever blessed morn!" in Goss's four parts. The book sets the verses for one voice over the keyboard, so their lower parts here are new; in G major at a moderate pace.

credits.arrangement: The chorus in Goss's four parts (Christmas Carols New and Old), adapted by Stackapella; the verses' lower parts by Stackapella, on the book's keyboard part

licence.words: public domain: Edward Caswall died at Edgbaston, 2 January 1878 (Julian's Dictionary of Hymnology, quoted at hymnary.org); first published in his The Masque of Mary, and Other Poems (1858), p. 259, in seven stanzas and a chorus (Julian); sung here as Christmas Carols New and Old prints them, in six verses and the chorus, verse 1 under the notes and verses 2 to 6 below them, with its spellings and capitals ("thro'", "Cherubim", "Divine", "Thine", "Thy", "Thee"). Verses 1, 2, 5 and 6 are sung, each with the chorus: verses 3 and 4 are the shepherds' question ("Say, ye holy Shepherds, say") and their answer ("As we watched at dead of night"), a pair that would make no sense apart, so the pair is left out and the hymn keeps its opening, the manger and its closing prayer, at about three minutes. The chorus is sung as the music prints it, "Hail! Thou ever blessed morn!", where the cue after each verse reads "Hail, thou ever-blessed, &c."
licence.tune: public domain: John Goss died 10 May 1880 (Wikipedia; hymnary.org gives 1800 to 1880); "Humility", the tune Goss wrote for these words, first published in Christmas Carols New and Old in 1871 (IMSLP: "Originally published in Christmas Carols New and Old in 1871 by Henry Bramley and John Stainer"; praise.org.uk agrees, and says the tune is named from the hymn's last word). The book's index (p. 183) gives "See amid the Winter snow" as No. XXX, words "The Rev. E. Caswall", air "Sir John Goss". The tune is sung note for note as printed: the verse from the solo line, the chorus from its top part
licence.arrangement: The page sets the verse for a solo voice ("Solo", with the footnote "Treble or Tenor, or alternately") on its own staff, marked Moderato, over a two-stave keyboard part marked Moderato and p, whose right hand doubles the tune (in places in minims where the tune has a dotted crotchet and a quaver) over an inner part, and whose left hand has a bass and, in places, a tenor; the chorus ("ff Chorus", p. 65) is printed in four voices on two staves, treble and alto on one, tenor and bass on the other, with no separate keyboard part. The book credits the air to Goss and names no other harmonizer (its music editor John Stainer died 1901; public domain). The verses' alto, tenor and bass are Stackapella's own, written on the keyboard part's chords and following its inner voices where they suit singers: the alto's G3, A3, B3 on "winter's snow" and "Lamb appears" and its B3, C4, D4, E4, then C4, C4, B3 in the last line are the keyboard's inner part, and the tenor's E3, F sharp 3, G3 on "winter's snow" and its suspension G3, F sharp 3, G3 on "-ternal years" are the left hand's. Where they differ from the keyboard: the alto takes E4 on "-mid" (the keyboard's inner C4 would be a bare fifth under the tune for 2 singers); line 2 is sung over G, D7, C over E, G over B, G over D and D (the keyboard: G, D over F sharp, C over E, G, then G over D, a C sharp neighbour note, D and D7 over C), so the bass sings G2, D3, E3, B2, D3 (the keyboard's G3, F sharp 3, E3, G3, D3) and no two parts move in octaves; line 3 takes line 1's parts, as the tune repeats (the keyboard puts B2 under its first chord and a D chord over F sharp under the held "-pears"); and every part sings one note a syllable, the keyboard's held and passing notes made into each syllable's chord. The chorus is Goss's four parts in his key, revoiced for 2 to 4 beginners so the duet and trio keep the chord's third. Goss's alto holds G4 or D4 under the tune through most of the chorus (a bare fifth on "Hail!", a fourth on "ev-" and "-demp-", an octave on the second "Hail" and on "Christ", a unison on "-lem" and "-hem"), so the alto and tenor exchange: on "Hail! Thou ever" the alto sings Goss's tenor, B3, B3, E4, D4, and the tenor the root, G3 (his alto's G4 an octave down); on "Hail, Redemption's" the alto sings B3, B3 (his D4, G4), then his tenor's E4, D4, and the tenor G3 throughout (his G3, G3, E4, D4); on "Christ is born in Bethlehem" the alto sings B3, B3, E4, E4, D4, C4, B3 (his D4, D4, E4, G4, F sharp 4, F sharp 4, G4) and the tenor G3, G3, G3, G3, F sharp 3, F sharp 3, G3 (his G3, G3, G3, E4, D4, C4, B3), the same chords. On "blessed" the alto sings C4 (his D4) and the tenor A3 (his C4), so the chord is F sharp, A, C over the bass's F sharp; on "happy" the alto sings C4 (his E4) and the tenor E3 (his C4). The bass sings bars 1 and 2 an octave lower (G2 for his G3, F sharp 2 for his F sharp 3), so the tenor's G3 doesn't double it in unison. One note a syllable in every lower part: the bass's quavers B2, C3 on "happy" become B2, and its D3, C3 under "-lem" become D3; on "Jerusalem" the lower parts move with the tune's dotted rhythm, Goss's crotchet chords (his alto D4, C sharp 4, D4; tenor B3, then quavers A3, G3, then F sharp 3; bass G2, A2, D3, C3) sung as A7 over G on "ru-" (alto C sharp 4, tenor A3, bass G2), A with a suspended fourth on "-sa-" (alto E4, tenor A3, bass A2) and D on "-lem" (alto F sharp 4, tenor A3, bass D3). There the alto crosses a third above the tune's held D4 at the end of the line, where Goss's alto doubles it, and the tenor takes the fifth, A3, so the leading tone isn't doubled; the alto then falls a fifth to B3 for "Christ", at the next line's start. Left as printed: the alto's D4 a fourth under the tune's G4 on the weak second beat of "blessed" and "happy" (Goss's alto), and Goss's last chord, which has no fifth (G2, B3, G4, G4), sung here with its fifth in the tenor (G2, D3, B3, G4). In each verse the alto and tenor exchange under "for" (the D7 chord): alto F sharp 4, tenor C4, then C4 on "us", so the alto has the chord's third and the duet sings thirds and sixths there. Breaths written in for beginners: each line's last minim gives up three quarters of a beat, except the song's last note
licence.source: Christmas Carols New and Old, the words edited by the Rev. Henry Ramsden Bramley, the music edited by Sir John Stainer (London and New York: Novello, Ewer and Co., undated; the complete edition of seventy carols, "Price Four Shillings", printed after Stainer's knighthood in 1888 and under the publisher's style Novello, Ewer and Co., so between 1888 and about 1898), No. XXX, "Hymn for Christmas Day", pp. 64 and 65, in G major (one sharp), common time, Moderato, sung here in its printed key (G); read from the Princeton Theological Seminary copy (bequeathed by Louis FitzGerald Benson) at archive.org/details/christ00bram/page/n69 (p. 64: verse 1, solo, over the keyboard) and n70 (p. 65: the chorus in four parts and verses 2 to 6), with the index, p. 183, at n188
